screens.title: Advanced Testing Techniques
screens.subtitle: Verify reverts, events, modifiers, and use expressive matchers for robust contracts

narration.text: Today you'll learn the advanced testing techniques that make smart contracts safer and more predictable. We move beyond simple assertions about state and return values to deliberate checks that transactions fail when they should, that events are emitted with exact arguments, and that modifiers correctly gate access. These patterns reduce risk: a test suite that confirms exact revert messages and event payloads catches logic and integration bugs early. You will see concrete examples using an Ownable contract and a small ERC-20 token. We'll cover how to assert reverts with a specific message, how to assert event emission and arguments using the to. emit matcher, and how to test modifiers like onlyOwner to ensure both success and failure paths are covered. By the end you will understand why negative tests matter, which common mistakes to avoid, and how to structure tests so they give high confidence before deployment. Think of these techniques as building a contract's safety net — they prove not only that the happy path works, but that edge cases are handled correctly. What failing condition will your next test catch?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Precise revert checks and event assertions give stronger guarantees about behavior and integration than simple success tests. They catch security and integration bugs early.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Advanced Testing Techniques
Advanced Testing Techniques
Verify reverts, confirm event payloads, and test modifiers with confidence.

This lesson teaches negative testing, event assertions, and modifier checks using Hardhat and Waffle's chai-ethers matchers. The examples that follow use an Ownable contract and a simple ERC-20 to ground concepts in code.

Tools

Outcome

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will implement tests that prove both successful and failing behavior. First, you will learn to write tests that assert specific revert messages. This skill matters because precise revert assertions catch the exact guard that failed, rather than only confirming a failure occurred. For example, you will write tests that assert an onlyOwner call reverts with the 'caller is not the owner' message. Second, you will verify event emission and arguments. Reliable event tests ensure that off-chain systems relying on logs receive the values you expect. Third, you will test modifiers, including both success and negative paths, so access control checks are enforced. Finally, you will apply chai-ethers/Waffle matchers for expressive assertions like to. be. revertedWith and to. emit(...). withArgs(...), improving test clarity and reducing flakiness. Each objective is tied to code examples and exercises using Ownable and a simplified ERC-20 so you practice both pattern and reasoning. Achieving these objectives will raise your contracts' safety and the trust engineers can place in them.

screens.title: Testing revert conditions
screens.subtitle: Confirm transactions fail where the contract should prevent them

narration.text: A revert condition is an explicit guard inside a contract that stops execution and undoes state changes when a precondition is not met. In Solidity these guards are often written with require, revert, or assert. Testing reverts means you must force the failing condition in a test and assert not only that the transaction reverted, but that it reverted for the intended reason. A precise example from the Ownable contract is transferOwnership: it has two guards, one that ensures only the owner can call the function, and another that prevents setting the zero address. In tests you exercise both failure paths: calling transferOwnership from a non-owner should revert with the string "Ownable: caller is not the owner", and calling it with the zero address should revert with "Ownable: new owner is the zero address". This ensures each require is present and correct. A common mistake is to use a generic to. be. reverted assertion without checking the message; that can mask which guard fired. Another frequent mistake is forgetting to await a transaction, which can cause tests to pass or throw unpredictably. Your takeaway: write a test for each explicit guard, force the failing input or signer, assert the exact message with to. be. revertedWith, and double-check that no state changed after the failure. How will you detect the guard that matters in your next contract?

keyIdea.title: Revert testing takeaway
keyIdea.text: Assert the exact revert message to verify the correct guard triggered and that no state changed.

content.html:
Definition
Testing revert conditions
Force failing inputs and assert exact error messages to prove guards exist and behave correctly.
Why this matters
  • Confirms preconditions are enforced and specific errors are returned.
  • Prevents silent failures where a different guard reverts the call.
  • Makes contract behavior explicit for off-chain error handling.
Common mistakes
Using to.be.reverted instead of checking the message, and forgetting to await state-changing calls. Both lead to brittle or misleading tests.
// test snippet (visual example)
await expect(ownable.connect(addr1).transferOwnership(addr2.address))
  .to.be.revertedWith("Ownable: caller is not the owner");

await expect(ownable.connect(owner).transferOwnership(ethers.constants.AddressZero))
  .to.be.revertedWith("Ownable: new owner is the zero address");
Check your understanding

If a test uses to.be.reverted and it passes, what additional assertion would you add to confirm the revert reason? Try asserting the exact message with to.be.revertedWith.

screens.title: to.be.reverted vs to.be.revertedWith
screens.subtitle: When to assert a generic revert and when to assert the exact message

narration.text: The two matchers, to. be. reverted and to. be. revertedWith, look similar but serve different purposes. to. be. reverted only checks that a transaction failed and that no state changes or events were committed. It is useful in very generic tests where you only need to ensure a call does not succeed but you do not control the callee's revert message. However, using this matcher alone is risky when your contract has multiple guards. A test that uses to. be. reverted may pass even if the wrong guard fired, hiding logic bugs. to. be. revertedWith checks that the transaction reverted with an exact message string. It confirms the intended require trigger fired and that the developer wrote a clear, specific message. Prefer to. be. revertedWith for your own contracts and when the guard message is part of the contract's contract. Use to. be. reverted only when the tested call comes from an external dependency or when the revert message cannot be relied on. A practical example is the Ownable transferOwnership tests: assert the owner mismatch message with to. be. revertedWith. A misconception to avoid: adding overly generic messages in require statements and tests relying on the generic check defeats the purpose — you should write specific messages and check them. The takeaway: aim for specificity in both contract messages and test assertions to reduce silent failures.

keyIdea.title: Matcher choice
keyIdea.text: Use to.be.revertedWith for your contracts' guards; reserve to.be.reverted for uncontrolled external calls.

content.html:
Comparison
to.be.reverted vs to.be.revertedWith
to.be.reverted
Asserts a transaction failed. Use when you don't control the callee's message or in very generic failure checks.
When to use
  • External library calls where messages vary.
  • Quick checks that a call is protected without message guarantees.
to.be.revertedWith
Asserts the exact revert message. Prefer this for your own contract guards to ensure the right precondition failed.
When to use
  • Testing require messages in your contract.
  • Ensuring correct guard and user-facing error strings.
Common pitfall

Relying on to.be.reverted hides which require fired. Always prefer specific messages for guards and assert them in tests.

screens.title: Testing modifiers and access control
screens.subtitle: Prove guards like onlyOwner behave for both allowed and disallowed callers

narration.text: Modifiers are reusable precondition blocks that run before a function body. Common examples include onlyOwner, onlyAdmin, or whenNotPaused. Testing modifiers is straightforward but essential: you must exercise both sides of the condition. For onlyOwner, test a successful call from the owner account and a failing call from a non-owner; assert the exact revert message in the failure case. The Ownable examples show transferOwnership and doSomethingImportant being called by owner and non-owner signers. Testing modifiers also requires attention to which signer sends the transaction because msg. sender is recorded from the active signer. A common error is using the default signer when you intended to test a different account, invalidating the test. Another point: when modifier logic updates state on success, assert final state after the successful call and confirm no change after the failed call. For reusable modifiers covering role checks, write a matrix of test cases: allowed role executes and produces expected state or event, disallowed role reverts with the correct message. This pattern scales to modifiers with more complex conditions; test each path separately so the modifier itself remains a small, well-covered contract surface.

keyIdea.title: Modifier testing
keyIdea.text: Always test both acceptance and rejection paths, using the correct signer and asserting final state or lack of state change.

content.html:
Definition
Testing modifiers and access control
Test matrix
  • Allowed signer: call succeeds, state change or event observed.
  • Disallowed signer: call reverts with the specific message.
Signer care
Always use connect(signer) to send transactions from different accounts when testing msg.sender dependent logic.
// modifier tests (visual example)
await expect(ownable.connect(owner).doSomethingImportant())
  .to.equal("Important task completed!");

await expect(ownable.connect(addr1).doSomethingImportant())
  .to.be.revertedWith("Ownable: caller is not the owner");
Key Takeaway

Test both sides of modifier checks and assert state or events on success and exact messages on failure.

screens.title: Event testing with to.emit(...).withArgs(...)
screens.subtitle: Assert that important events are logged with correct arguments

narration.text: Events are the contract's log messages that off-chain systems rely on. Testing them verifies that front-ends and indexers receive the right payload. The Waffle matcher to. emit(contract, "EventName"). withArgs(...) ensures the event was emitted during a transaction and that its arguments match exactly. For example, when transferOwnership succeeds the OwnershipTransferred(previousOwner, newOwner) event should be emitted with both addresses. In tests you call transferOwnership as the owner and assert the event and arguments. Also test negative paths: when transfer fails, ensure the transaction reverts and no event is observed; although a revert prevents events, explicitly asserting the revert message is the most direct confirmation. Be mindful of indexed parameters: withArgs still expects the values you care about; when matching topics, pass the exact address values. Another practical concern is signer correctness — the event often contains msg. sender or previousOwner values that depend on who sent the transaction. Confirm the signer used to send the transaction matches the expected event payload. Finally, use event tests to validate emitted data for things like Transfer and Approval in ERC-20, ensuring off-chain balances align with on-chain logs.

keyIdea.title: Event assertion
keyIdea.text: Use to.emit(...).withArgs(...) to confirm both that an event occurred and that its arguments match expected values.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Event testing with to.emit(...).withArgs(...)
Why events matter
Events provide the canonical source for off-chain systems. Tests ensure logs match expected values so explorers and front-ends behave correctly.
Signer and topics
Use the correct signer for transactions because event fields often reflect msg.sender or previous owner values.
// event test example
await expect(ownable.connect(owner).transferOwnership(addr1.address))
  .to.emit(ownable, "OwnershipTransferred")
  .withArgs(owner.address, addr1.address);

// ERC-20 transfer example
await expect(token.connect(owner).transfer(addr1.address, 100))
  .to.emit(token, "Transfer")
  .withArgs(owner.address, addr1.address, 100);
Pro tip

When matching indexed parameters, pass the expected address values; withArgs will compare topics as provided.

screens.title: Negative testing workflow
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step pattern for writing negative tests

narration.text: A reliable negative test follows a consistent workflow. First, determine the guard you want to exercise: a require that enforces a non-zero address, a balance check, or an access control modifier. Second, set up the test state so the guard triggers: choose the signer or provide the invalid input that violates the precondition. Third, call the function and assert the revert with the exact message using to. be. revertedWith. Fourth, assert no state change after the failed call: query relevant storage variables and compare to pre-call values. Fifth, run complementary positive tests that exercise the happy path and assert the expected state change and events. Applying this pattern reduces flakiness and ensures every guard is tested on both sides. A common misconception is that a single revert assertion covers both guard presence and correct state handling; it does not. Always confirm the precondition prevented any partial updates. Use this five-step flow as a template when writing tests for require checks, modifier gates, and ERC-20 allowance/balance failures. Negative testing workflow means follow a five-step workflow: identify guard, set state, assert revert message, confirm no state change, and complement with a positive test.. In practical terms, a step-by-step pattern for writing negative tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Negative test pattern

Process Flow
Negative testing workflow
1. Identify guard
Which require or modifier should block the call?
2. Set failing state
Choose signer or invalid input that triggers the guard.
3. Assert revert
Use to.be.revertedWith with the exact message.
4. Confirm no state change
Read storage values and ensure nothing changed.
5. Complement with positive test
Run the success case and assert expected state and events.
Check

Ask: did the guard prevent any partial updates? If yes, the negative test is complete.

screens.title: ERC-20 testing: transfer and transferFrom
screens.subtitle: Validate transfers, approvals, events, and failure modes

narration.text: A focused exercise is testing ERC-20 transfer, approve, and transferFrom. The MyERC20 contract emits Transfer and Approval events and enforces non-zero addresses and sufficient balances/allowances. Start by deploying the contract with an initial supply and assert the deployer received that supply. Test transfer from owner to another account and assert balances and the Transfer event arguments. Then test failure cases: transferring more than balance should revert with the balance error message, and transferring to the zero address should revert with the zero address message. For approvals, call approve and assert allowance and the Approval event, then test that approving the zero address reverts. For transferFrom: first approve a spender, then have the spender call transferFrom and assert balances, allowance decrement, and event emission. Also write negative tests for insufficient allowance, insufficient balance, and zero addresses. Remember to await transactions and use the correct signers: connect(owner) for owner actions, connect(spender) for transferFrom. These tests validate both token integrity and the events relied upon by wallets and explorers. ERC-20 testing: transfer and transferFrom means cover success and failure for transfer, approve, and transferfrom; assert events, balances, and allowance changes precisely..   .to.emit(token, "Transfer")

  .to.be.revertedWith("ERC20: transfer amount exceeds balance");

screens.title: Common testing mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Pitfalls that make tests brittle or misleading

narration.text: There are recurring mistakes that make test suites unreliable. The first is vague revert assertions: using to. be. reverted instead of to. be. revertedWith allows incorrect revert reasons to slip through. Second, forgetting to await transactions can cause tests to behave nondeterministically; always await state-changing calls. Third, using the wrong signer for calls or event checks will produce unexpected msg. sender values and mismatched event arguments. Fourth, ignoring negative tests and only writing happy-path tests leaves critical guards untested. Fifth, assuming a revert means no logs were emitted without checking the state — while a revert does undo state and events, explicitly asserting revert messages clarifies intent. To avoid these issues, always write both positive and negative tests, assert exact messages, await transactions, and carefully connect the intended signer. When in doubt, add one more assertion: check the state before and after the call so you can prove no partial update occurred. These small habits dramatically improve your test clarity and security coverage. Testing pitfalls and fixes

Missing await

screens.title: Structuring tests for readability and coverage
screens.subtitle: Arrange tests so intent and coverage are clear

narration.text: A readable test suite helps other engineers understand intent and ensures coverage. Use describe blocks to group behaviors by contract and function, use beforeEach to deploy fresh instances and set up signers, and name it blocks to state the expected outcome clearly. For example, group Ownable tests under describe("Ownable") and use nested describes for transferOwnership and doSomethingImportant. In beforeEach deploy the contract and assign owner, addr1, and addr2 so every test starts from a known state. Within each it block follow the arrange-act-assert pattern: arrange the state, act by sending the transaction with the correct signer and awaited promise, then assert state or events. Include negative cases immediately after the happy path to make the difference obvious. Keep assertions focused and atomic: one expectation per logical outcome when possible. This structure also helps when adding tests later, such as for new modifiers. Finally, include short comments or a one-line summary in each test if the assertion is non-obvious. Clear structure reduces friction during audits and makes coverage reports meaningful. Structuring tests for readability and coverage means use describe and beforeeach, follow arrange-act-assert, and place negative cases beside happy paths for clarity and maintainability.. In practical terms, arrange tests so intent and coverage are clear. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Structuring tests
